Issued at 804 AM EDT Thu Oct 22 2026

Confidence is high that the peaceful weather described above will 
persist into the long term forecast period. Forecast guidance 
collectively resolves a mid/upper level ridge building into the 
Greater Ohio River Valley this weekend. Synoptic-scale subsidence 
downstream of the ridge axis will keep skies clear and keep a 
surface high pressure system nearby. The northerly orientation of 
the flow aloft and the light/variable nature of the surface-level 
winds will limit the amount of meaningful advection realized over 
the CWA. So, given the dryness of the antecedent airmass, there are 
no meaningful rain chances in the forecast for the next 7 days. 

Ridging patterns like this favor efficient diurnal radiative and 
mixing processes, and those processes will be the primary factor 
governing Eastern Kentucky's sensible weather conditions through 
early next week. Bountiful solar insolation and nocturnal ridge-
valley splits should yield 25-35 degree diurnal temperature ranges 
each day. Subtle geopotential height rises suggest that Saturday and 
Sunday's temperatures could fall on the higher end of the forecast 
guidance envelope, and highs should reach widespread readings in the 
the low/mid 70s each day. Lows will be more terrain-dependent, with 
ridgetops remaining in the 40s as colder air pools in the valleys 
after dark. The most sheltered and shaded valleys will see 
temperatures cool down into the mid 30s, and patchy frost cannot be 
entirely ruled out in these hollows. In the broader valleys, the 
presence of rivers, lakes, creeks, and streams will favor fog 
formation as lows drop into the upper 30s/lower 40s. More locations 
should see fog than frost amidst the aforementioned warming trend, 
but trends in afternoon dewpoint observations will need to be 
monitored closely. If diurnal mixing is deep enough to mix down the 
dry air aloft, the areal coverage of frost could be greater than 
what is currently included in the forecast grids. It would not be 
surprising if 20-30 degree dewpoint depressions are realized, and 
the blended NBM guidance used to populate the long term forecast 
grids is likely too moist. Small differences can make a big impact 
when it comes to forecasting crossover temps and fog/frost, but 
neither of these weather conditions would produce significant 
impacts. 

Such quiet weather can only persist for so long though, and the 
ridging pattern is poised to gradually break down next week. As an 
upper level trough ejects into the Plains on Monday, the ridge over 
the Ohio Valley will flatten out. The resultant height falls point 
towards a slight decrease in temperatures, and the flow aloft will 
shift towards a more westerly and then southwesterly orientation by 
Tuesday. This shift will introduce relatively greater amounts of 
moisture to the column and thus some cloud cover back into the 
forecast. Model spread begins to increase beyond then, as there are 
differing solutions surrounding the trajectory and evolution of that 
ejecting trough. Hazardous weather appears unlikely with this first 
system, as there will not be much low-level moisture return out 
ahead of its arrival and it will likely lose its upper atmospheric 
support as time progresses. Some guidance suggests that there could 
be some light precipitation on Wednesday, but ensemble probabilities 
for measurable precipitation remain less than 15%. Thus, the 
greatest changes in the forecast associated with this late-period 
system will likely be tied to that increase in cloud cover. Expect 
slightly cooler highs and slightly warmer lows as those clouds 
modify the diurnal radiation budget, but temperatures should remain 
in the same general upper 60s/lower 70s and low/mid 40s range.
